title: Jonas Hanway's umbrella
hook: A London man carried an umbrella for 30 years and was jeered for most of them.
peek: In 1750s London, umbrellas were thought fit only for women. Jonas Hanway, a traveller and writer, carried one anyway, and kept doing it for about 30 years despite the taunts. By the end of his life men carried them too, and people called them Hanways.
lede: Umbrellas had long been used in hot countries as sunshades, but in 18th-century London a man with one looked odd. They were seen as a lady's accessory, and a gentleman caught in rain was expected to take a carriage. Jonas Hanway, who had travelled widely, started carrying an umbrella around 1750 and refused to stop.

bullets.text: As a merchant, Hanway had travelled through Russia and Persia, where shades and parasols were in common use. He is said to have brought the habit home and saw no reason why a man should get wet.
Hanway was mocked in the street, and the loudest critics were said to be hackney coachmen. Every rainy day was good business for them, and a man who walked under his own cover was a lost fare.
Hanway kept up the habit for around 30 years, until his death in 1786. He was not the very first man in London with an umbrella, but he was the one people remembered for it.
By the end of the 1700s, men in London carried umbrellas without remark. For a while they were nicknamed Hanways after the man who had put up with the teasing.
